来自抢先版[Beat Hazard 3]评测 界面：UI字体需要美化。 音乐：前几作的专辑已经回归可以游玩。 敌人：更多更大的boss，以及更好的光影效果。 玩法：战机按右键可以变形，用来对付盔甲类敌人。 视觉：新增加了3D可视化效果与更夸张的爆炸效果。 创新：本作新加入了宇宙星系与母舰系统（可自定义）。 便捷：可以正式使用实时音乐来游玩，不用下载即可游玩 背景：使用每一个独立的星球皮肤作为背景可以增加极大的代入感。 建议：更大战斗区域，更多的视效选择，更多的养成玩法，内置音乐编辑器。

Alright, I guess I’ve played enough to make a review. For context I’ve played this series since the first game (which is my 7th most played game on steam) and at one point was quiet good at it. Like in the top 200 players in the world and in the top 10 for a handful of categories. Of course this was when I was young and full of hope before the harsh realities of the world, aging, and years of recreational drug use ironed out all the wrinkles in my grey matter leaving me a smoothbrained ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, but I digress. Beat Hazard, for those who don’t know, is basically the classic arcade game ‘Asteroids’ if it ripped a rail of cocaine and amphetamines before downing a case of pre-ban Four Loko. It is very much in the bullet hell genre. The twist is that every level is generated based on music that you provide. Enemy ships numbers, types, spawn times, attack patterns, and bosses are all determined by what song you feed into the system and are consistent to each track so that you can compete with friends and strangers without too much RNG ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ stealing your rightful place at the top of the leaderboard. This system is very fun 80% of the time. The other 20% of the time you get a combination of factors that make a song hellish to complete at higher difficulties. Luckily, there is a much larger degree of difficulty scaling than in previous entries, so you can fine tune it to your tastes. Or you can be an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ like me and immedietly crank it to 2000% difficulty out of the gate and be very frustrated the first couple hours. Which is not even to say that 2000% difficulty is impossible, but (at least in my case) I started with a painfully slow, big ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ship that handled like it was the grandchild of a cadillac and a boat whose parents were both retired NFL linebackers. It did not move gracefully to say the least, drifting with a ton of momentum whenever it moved and taking longer to get moving from a stop than a white lady playing candy crush at a traffic light. This combined with it’s hunking size made dodging bullets and manuvering around enemies basically impossible. I hated the game the entire time I had to use this ship. That said, each song you finish will offer you a randomly generated ship that you can take as a replacement. It took probably 10 or so tracks, but I finally got something I liked and it was good times from then on. It would be nice if there was maybe an option of a few different ship archetypes to choose from so you can start with something that reflects your desired play style rather than hoping to get one from RNGesus. Additionally, there is a nice system that lets you spend points to fine tune several aspects of any ship like acceleration, top speed, deceleration, pick up force, bullet spread and damaged etc. This helps tremendously with the whole ‘having fun’ thing. The big new addition here is the Galaxy mode. Basically you pick however many artists you want and it will generate a big campaign map that you can play solo or online with friends. Each artist is a star cluster, every album a solar system, and each song a planet. You fly between them in an upgradeable mothership conquering systems and gathering resources. It keeps a neat little line to show your travel paths and is a nice way to have you engage with songs you may have forgotten you have. I’ve rediscovered a ton of tracks that I really like that I haven’t listened to in years between this and the random song option. If you don’t have your own files there is also an option to use Spotify with like 5 million tracks or something. This is all presuming that you have a collection of music files from the dark days before music streaming. If you don’t have your own files there is an open mic feature that allows you to play stuff from your streaming service of choice as well as a bunch of songs tailor made for the game. As an aside, these are probably the best original tracks of the series in my opinion. Beat Hazard 3 is still in early access and is only on phase 3 of 6 current planned content updates, so there is plenty of chance for feedback to address balance and interface issues. The game is made by one friendly guy living in the UK, so I’m much more willing to give grace on some of my gripes. This game has a million times more heart than whatever the latest Call of Duty Activision managed to ♥♥♥♥ out in between sexually harassing the women working there. THAT SAID I will now directly address Starg, the developer: Hey bud. Love the game. I’m sure you’re aware of some of the technical issues that are still in the game like the buggy menus in the galaxy mode and mothership editor, or the framerate ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the bed when ships load in for the first time or too many explosions happen at once. I don’t need to complain about those as that’s the kind of stuff that gets fixed in the polish phase of development. HOWEVER, I have a few requests. First off is an in game menu to let me tweak the colors of enemy projectiles. I know there are three types of energy ball now and each has a different effect, but I can’t see the red one for ♥♥♥♥ most of the time. You already have RGB sliders for the mothership and galaxy background and this has been editable in the past through an ini file. Please add the option. Also I think it would benefit new players tremendously to have a bestiary, per say, so learn what each enemy type is and what their potential arsenal is. Lastly, let me build my own ship from scratch. You can tie it into the galaxy mode or have players earn different parts from songs or scrapping collected ships, but I want to make something that fits my playstyle and my aesthetic taste. It was in 2 and I would love to see that expanded on. You can even use the same existing assets. Just let me slap that sum'♥♥♥♥♥ together myself piece by piece, you know? Also, let me select the difficulty when I’m doing a ship challenge directly from the ship detail screen instead of just using whatever the last setting I played with. Also the Crusader Turrets are mad overpowered, please do not change that. Again, love the game. Toodles. Now back to the plebs who have read this far for some reason. Having gone back and played some Beat Hazard 2 I am now confident in saying that 3 is dramatically less fun. The forced use of the Dark Beam as the only method to penetrate shields really drags down the pacing and that's when it works. Playing boss rush I encountered a ship whose THIRD level of shields simply refused to break no matter how much I blasted them. I believe that this game will eventually get to a place where it is a delight to play, but it simply is not at this time. Go buy BH1 or 2 instead. -Steffy B da beat fiend As an addendum, the other review at the top of the page has a very solid point. The game suffers from a massive readability issue. There have been countless times where I have died to something that was completely imperceptible to me. Some percentage of that has to me just not being good, but a good chunk of the time there is literally nothing visible to have caused my death. This makes the game completely unfun at max difficulty. So far it seems like the game is most fun at like 700-1000% difficulty for me. As it is now, there is draw to compete for high scores or to play at the top skill level. The top difficulty used to be pulse pounding and adrenaline fueled, but now it's just a frustrating mess. It isn't challenging, it is just difficult. The lack of the old perk system is also a major detriment as well. Not being able to trade off things like pick up rates for combo multipliers, or give up your spare lives for more drops leaves little reason to experiment.

I have played a lot of the first two games in this series. This entry is pretty disappointing compared to those. First, Galaxy mode is fairly tedious with the fuel mechanic. Second, the general upgrades are mechanically a step down from the second game. Third, navigation of one's mp3 collection ingame is tedious. It is easier to simply use the file Explorer option but if you have your collection on a server or something it is quite cumbersome. The ship system in this is a big downgrade from the previous title. While I do prefer the upgrade system of 3, the ships in 2 were more interesting and varied. Plus there was built in workshop support for limitless ship designs. I also greatly dislike the general gameplay of this compared to the second game. The shadow beam to destroy enemy shields is a horribly thought out mechanic and it adds a layer of complexity that does not work well given how chaotic this game gets. Get the second game over this one at the time of this review. It is the superior title.

Much of the design choices in [i]Beat Hazard 3[/i] do not justify its price, let alone do it any favors when compared to its two predecessors. Cold Beam Games has yet to realize the true nature of bullet-hell video games. Instead, it concentrates on visual feedback as it relates to the music currently played and attempts to program that into gameplay. The question is — how does this product demonstrate itself as a competent video game and music visualizer? What illustrates the development's lack of focus on its insertion into the shoot 'em up genre is how easily players' ships can effortlessly become lost when large and small, along with their projectiles that share varying sizes, swiftly fill the screen with hundreds to near thousands of multi-dimensional, digital vomit. Not a single ship available to the player stands out enough to justify violent storms of enemies and all their projectiles, and what makes matters worse is that the cooldown for the beam (which is responsible for clearing excessive projectiles on the screen) lasts longer than the duration of the beam's lifetime. With strobe lights enabled, by default, players will have to squint their eyes and fidget around the screen in schizophrenic intervals. Note that, although this game routinely accesses users' files and the Internet, it additionally and routinely fails to recognize tracks and ends them when short periods of silence are observed or continue them, in a playlist-like manner, when tracks play back-to-back without an indicator of their end. It is no wonder why some antivirus software attempts to kill execution files similar to Beat Hazard 3's when intrusiveness and ineffectiveness come together so frequently in these products. In summary, there are much more entertaining and functioning space shooters and music visualizers that are more than deserving of their time (some even being free of cost) when compared to this product. It becomes apparent that this game's Internet features and niche community were its selling points; much of the gameplay is repetitive and depends on user-generated content to supply the game's replayability and return on investment. Due to this, it is unclear whether Beat Hazard 3 needed more time on the drawing board or should have never left the drawing board in the first place.

《危险节奏3宇宙争霸》 哇呜，2到3这次进化真是肉眼可见的大变革，先从2D变3D建模，画面更加酷炫，代价是暂时无法通过创意工坊DIY战机。 一、核心玩法。 一直没变，但系统重心绑定到新玩法“银河战争”上。 根据歌单生成一个庞大银河系，其中每首曲子都是一个星球。 玩家控制一艘可自定义模块的母舰，在星际空间内跃迁旅行，驾驶形形色色的品牌战机获取“燃料”与“纳米材料”（简单理解就是前作强化用的金钱啦），并根据得分高低来决定星球的占领权。——本地歌单不能分享给朋友？在线银河貌似只能用流媒体文件，没有支持国内的网易云之类，哈哈哈。 鼓励高分冲榜，单曲难度上限也很贴心的增加到2000%！——而且，这次无尽模式难度似乎随时间递增更快，倍率数值更直观。 二，强化与成长。 挑战高难度，火力不足怎么办？ 母舰建造，即是我方局外增益，目前装饰外观多，实用功能模块较少，估计是还没做？ 可选副武器，新增四种：清屏（地毯式轰炸），龙息（破盾毒雾），复仇女神（穿透回旋镖），毒蛇（追踪型闪电链）。 实战中感觉有点像功能卡牌，在特定的包围局势用使用某种副武器，轻松打破困局，弹药掉落补给充足，几乎不用担心余粮问题。 强化数值分为5常规+2超载，非常非常烧钱，但肯定物有所值，初期优先考虑。——比如忽悠炮的数量，护盾的持久，强化后简直是质变。 副武器最多携带3种（选择困难症激活），注意每架战机都需要单独配置，小心习惯性按错键。 三，战机强化大变革。 战机可通过暗影任务或购买获取的“调整点”随意改变各种属性，每项上下浮动最大6个档位——真的有必要降低吗？削弱自己也要消耗强化点？？之前反而增加改造点数。 每架战机单独结算，买满40点调整值上限需要4000纳米，更肝了（购买后概不退款！），500%难一首歌带加成也就奖励二三百，所以初期只能集中强化极少量顺手战机用以刷钱。 新增主属性“弹射概率”很有趣，高难度下有奇效，只可意会。 四，弹幕类型调整。 敌人除了经典的秒杀红色光球、紫色光束，禁攻的绿色，新增了减速效果的蓝色，个别精英敌机还可以放出超大范围的新星光球，延时破裂集束蛋，以及一长串细小干扰弹幕，更加防不胜防！ 莫慌，作为平衡，我方经典副武器冷光（cold beam笑）变为常规武器“暗黑光束”，使用限制只有充能CD，可以消除触碰到的所有敌方弹幕，并且是破除敌机能量护盾的唯一手段（护盾完全免疫常规弹幕！流氓啊！！！）。 总结： BH3绝非敷衍续作，整体设计思路与细节打磨都有考虑如何让经典模式变得更“好玩”，低难度依旧惬意，高难度下多兵种搭配，海量敌机考验玩家反应与操作技术，自虐向打飞机高手狂喜。 建议：爆炸音效还是太出戏了，能不能像《节奏盒子》那样改成B-box等等，搭配BGM效果更佳？

This is a neat idea, but the game doesn't deliver on it at all. The music has basically nothing to do with the gameplay. Both the game systems and the music connections are obtuse and frustrating to use. It's not even particularly good as a shooter if the music did matter. There's lots of random knobs to turn but none of them do anything worth turning. They basically just took a middling shooter, added a metric ton of RNG, and timed the power of your shots to the beat. It looks neat often enough, but it's deeply confusing that a game company decided to make fun of themselves for their own seizure inducing graphics.

I really want to like this game. I love the first two. But the UI is very hard to use, the open mic system doesn't feel good to use and the game feels like it doesn't want you to play it sometimes with how hard it can be to navigate menus etc. It could definitely be saved by patches because the core game here is solid - fighting enemies and bosses feels fun and exciting.

I wish I could say its good, but it just isn't currently. The open mic system fails pretty often, either not detecting the song, or detecting it incorrectly and thinking it is something entirely different. The galaxy mode has promise, but it currently works terribly. The game can for some reason identify most tracks played from spotify (when it works correctly) yet when building a galaxy, 90% of the artists I searched for just weren't there. That is another problem, you cannot add specific tracks to your galaxy, only an artist or a genre. I don't know about most people, but most of my music collection is single songs from different artists, not entire catalogues of a few artists. Having to add stuff this way makes the galaxy extremely bloated and difficult to get to any track you actually want to play. Why can't we just paste a spotify link for the game to accept as the track? Keep the annoying spotify browser tab system, but have it launch to the link you provide, and keep the record attached to it, that way there wouldn't be any failed detections, and you could build a galaxy exactly how you want it to be. Each planet/moon has a specific spotify link inserted by the creator that opens the page for the player. I like playing the game, it is fun, but it feels like any amount of fun you get comes with 5-10 minutes of frustration.

Beat Hazard 3, developed and published by Cold Beam Games, takes the series’ signature concept of turning music into gameplay and expands it into a much larger and more ambitious experience. At its heart, it remains a twin-stick space shooter where every song influences enemy behavior, attack intensity, visual effects, and overall pacing. However, this installment goes beyond being a simple music-reactive arcade game by introducing progression systems, galaxy exploration, and deeper customization that make it feel like a complete adventure rather than a collection of isolated stages. The most compelling aspect of the game is how effectively it transforms personal music into meaningful gameplay. Every track becomes a unique battlefield generated from the rhythm, volume, and energy of the song being played. Fast-paced electronic music can create relentless waves of enemies and spectacular explosions, while slower tracks often result in more measured encounters. This dynamic relationship between audio and gameplay ensures that no two sessions feel exactly alike. Players are encouraged to experiment with different genres and playlists, discovering how various musical styles influence the flow of combat. One of the major additions to the formula is the galaxy system. Instead of selecting songs one by one from a menu, players travel through a procedurally generated universe built from their music library. Albums are transformed into star systems while individual songs become destinations to explore and conquer. This feature adds a sense of discovery and progression that was largely absent in earlier entries. It cleverly turns a music collection into a personal map of the galaxy, giving players an incentive to revisit forgotten songs and explore their libraries in a completely new way. Combat itself remains highly satisfying. The controls are responsive, and the screen quickly fills with lasers, enemy ships, projectiles, and massive explosions. New mechanics such as the Fold ability add more tactical options, allowing players to escape dangerous situations or reposition themselves during intense firefights. Combined with a variety of weapons, upgrades, and unlockable equipment, the action offers enough depth to remain engaging over long play sessions. While the game can be enjoyed casually, it also provides plenty of challenge for players who enjoy mastering difficult arcade shooters. Visually, Beat Hazard 3 is an impressive spectacle. The game embraces bright colors, vibrant particle effects, and music-driven visualizers that constantly react to the soundtrack. Battles often resemble a combination of a space shooter and a live music visualization program, creating an atmosphere unlike most games in the genre. The enhanced 3D presentation gives enemy ships and environments greater detail, making the universe feel more alive than in previous installments. Watching the battlefield erupt in synchronization with the music is consistently entertaining and serves as one of the game’s biggest attractions. Another noteworthy improvement is the expanded support for music sources. The game is designed to work not only with local music files but also with audio from various external sources. This flexibility makes the concept much more practical for modern players who primarily use streaming services. The ability to generate gameplay from virtually any music source ensures that the experience remains fresh and adaptable regardless of how players choose to listen to their favorite songs. The progression systems also deserve praise. Exploring the galaxy, collecting resources, improving ships, and unlocking new content gives players long-term goals beyond chasing high scores. These additions provide a satisfying sense of advancement and help distinguish Beat Hazard 3 from more traditional arcade shooters. The game rewards continued exploration and experimentation, making it easy to spend dozens of hours discovering new combinations of music and gameplay. The game is not without some drawbacks. The sheer amount of visual activity can occasionally make it difficult to track enemy attacks, especially during particularly energetic songs. New players may also find the number of systems and progression mechanics somewhat overwhelming compared to the simplicity of earlier entries. Additionally, because gameplay quality can vary depending on the chosen music, some songs naturally produce more exciting encounters than others. Nevertheless, these issues are relatively minor compared to the creativity and replay value the game offers. Beat Hazard 3 succeeds because it takes a unique idea and develops it into something far more substantial than a novelty. By combining music visualization, arcade shooting, exploration, progression, and customization into a cohesive package, it delivers an experience that feels both familiar and refreshingly original. Whether players want to enjoy a few quick battles or invest time exploring an entire music-generated galaxy, the game offers enough content and variety to keep them engaged for a very long time. Beat Hazard 3 is a highly inventive and content-rich evolution of the music-driven shooter formula. Its impressive galaxy system, expanded customization, excellent music integration, and addictive gameplay make it one of the strongest entries in the series and a standout title for fans of rhythm-inspired action games. Rating: 8/10

I don't appreciate anything they've added since the very first game, except maybe the 'desktop audio' support, since I no longer collect mp3s. The one feature I've been looking for is "everyone gets the same level when they play the same song" and as far as I can tell, it's never been considered for implementation. The interface is still a mess, visuals are horrendous and not customizable in any way. Imagine if you could tune the visuals like a winamp visualizer; throw your own image files in there for sprites and such. Still the same blinding y2k era palette, fonts and sprites. There's so much here now that interferes with a 'pure' music gaming competitive experience. Did your opponent use the same visual intensity? The same ship? The same level as you through the game's progression? Invest in the same skill points? Use any weird trick to distort or modify the desktop audio to manipulate the levels? Maybe they started their song after the intro, and used the first 20 seconds of the next track to boost their damage output at the very end of the round? Why even have a leaderboard or lock progression behind beating other players when there's all these factors to consider. I just want to know if they played through the song as well as I did. Or just disable the online features completely (there goes song identification tho). Every song dumps a random ship on you, but even if you play the same song as someone else it's not guaranteed you'll get the same stats. This game currently benefits from existing alone and unchallenged in a seriously niche market. I wish I had more options, but I'll continue to support anyone endeavoring in the 'gameplay powered by your audio' space. Get it on a sale. Thanks for reading.

I honestly can't believe I'm writing a bad review for this game, but the settings for Beat Hazard 3 are just [b]absolutely atrocious[/b]. There are problems in the earlier Beat Hazard games but they're never as bad as they are here. The main issue is that rebinding controls is the biggest headache in the world and unlike [b]ANY OTHER GAME I'VE EVER PLAYED[/b]. In order to rebind your controls, the game will prompt you to press whatever key you want for each function [b]in succession[/b]. So it'll say like "Up" and you press "W," then it says "Down" and you press "D." Whatever. Then it'll get to like Special Weapon 1, Special Weapon 2, Special Weapon 3 and you just have to hope and pray you'll remember what you set those to. I mean, for ♥♥♥♥'s sake, this is 2026 and we can't just have a [b]LIST[/b] of key binds, like every other game that's ever been made on the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ planet? This ♥♥♥♥'s obviously meant to cater to controller users but I can't imagine that it works better for them without a list as well. So why is this a bad thing? Well namely when you're assigning weapons to your ship, it'll ask you to put a weapon in slot 1, slot 2, slot 3, but it won't tell you what key you have bound to those. So when you play the game and you're in a pinch and use Mouse 2 to activate the super bomb....[b]OOOOOOOPS! Mouse 2 doesn't do anything![/b] And you can't just simply rebind [i]one[/i] key, you have to go through the whole rigmarole and do all of them in order, which means you better remember each and every key that you want bound to each function, don't forget a thing or you'll have to do it again once you play the game and see that it's not to you're liking! Now let's talk about the issue when you have a friend playing with you in party mode. So it's just you and one other friend using two different ships, how bad can that be? Well, if your friend has different weapons on his ship than what you have...[b]OOOOOPS! He can't use those weapons![/b] You're restricted to what weapons the host has on his ship, which means if I have bombs, missiles, and the shield on my ship, and he has drones, flamethrower, and sentry turret on his, he literally can't use ANY weapon except the primary fire bullets. There's [u]zero[/u] organization for ships. It lists ships under different brands but I have no idea what differences there are; one brand is like for big ships and one is for small, fast ones, but I have no idea about any others. There's a "favorite" system but during the course of gameplay you'll acquire approximately 70 zillion ships, and you never know what they do or what random weapons they've been assigned that you'll have to alter later. If a friend is playing, how the hell is he going to know what ship he'd like to use? It's complete guesswork. I have like over 200 ships and I only stuck to two that worked for me. New to BH3 are these new features where, unlike the previous games, you have to upgrade your main mothership to expand the hangar to allow for more ships, upgrade warp core drives or whatever to travel to different 'galaxies' I think. This is so that you play on other people's 'galaxies' which are just gigantic playlists of hundreds if not thousands of songs from albums you've never heard and probably couldn't care less about. It's not mandatory to play but you don't get a certain type of upgrade currency if you don't play them (alien blueprints or research points I think), which just means if you want to 100% the game you'll have to play other people's crap music in gigantic galaxies with thousands of songs. What the ♥♥♥♥, I don't want to play other people's music, their tastes aren't my own. And I get that if I don't want to play their music I can just play arcade mode on my own, which is what I do, but I just feel like all that effort was a total waste of time. Gameplay-wise this is essentially the same as the previous BHs except now there's a "dark beam" which is a black laser that's required to break shields. At first I thought it added more strategy and depth to the gameplay but what this really means is that you have to max out your dark beam duration and minimize its recharge time. Especially where for some reason the developer thought it was a good idea to give missiles shields. Imagine being surrounded in a twin-sticks shooter and you have to take out shields of other ships imminently closing in and firing missiles at you that also have shields when you have a limited amount of time to use the dark beam. It sounds like it adds depth to the gameplay but really it just adds frustration. Then there's still the problem with screen shake and just too much visual noise on the screen. This has been prevalent since the first BH and maybe it's just because I'm an old man but there's so much that's visually distracting that it's hard to focus on what's coming right up into your face to kill you. This isn't just limited to the insanely bright lights for no reason, but I'll also include the random background rocks and mechanical debris that isn't actually hazardous yet nonetheless looks like you'll collide with it. Oh yeah and how do you close the game out? By pressing Escape on the main menu, right? Like every other game? Nope! Guess what that does? That resets your game to windowed mode and changes the base resolution, which always ♥♥♥♥♥ up the game for me. Then there's not being able to remove the Beat Hazard 3 soundtrack from your tracklist at all, so every time you scroll to find something new to play you always have to see Comma King, Eric Mclure, Red Shirt Theory, etc. in your list of artists and I'm like "Who tthe hell are these guys? Oh, it's the stupid BH3 artists." This game also just randomly rebinds your controls without asking you and with the above-mentioned problems, it's a real pain in the ass. There are so many easily fixed and yet still unresolved problems that really spoil this game. In basically all aspects apart from the look of the ships and the ability to tweak certain features on your ship, BH3 is a straight downgrade from BH2. I wish the visual fidelity of this game could be transferred over to BH2 (and have those annoying yellow missile spamming ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ removed from BH2) instead of this game. I get that this game is made by essentially one person, but that's why you get QA, you need multiple hands working on a project so it doesn't become this clusterf*ck. And hire people who won't kiss your ass. Or maybe he did get feedback and just didn't listen, I don't know. But I recommend against this unless, after being out for a couple of years the dev randomly decides to improve the aspects that I mention (doubtful).
